decision.explanation: An antiderivative is -1/\sin(2x). Evaluating at the bounds gives -1/\sin(\pi/2)+1/\sin(\pi/4)=-1+\sqrt{2}.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{8}$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /8}^{\pi /4}\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}{|}_{\sqrt{2}/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}-1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since cot²(x)=cos²(x)/sin²(x), the integrand simplifies to cos(x)+csc²(x). Integrating gives sin(x)-cot(x)+C, which is option e.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that ${cot}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
